hook: The gold in your ring|came from a *collision*

lines.say: August 17th, 2017. Detectors in the US and Italy feel a tiny ripple in space itself. A gravitational wave.
shots: q: LIGO detector arms aerial (public domain)
line art: ripple spreading through grid

lines.say: It came from two dead stars, neutron stars, spiraling into each other about a hundred and thirty million light-years away.
shots: q: neutron stars merging animation (NASA public domain)

lines.say: Less than two seconds after the wave, telescopes caught a flash of gamma rays. Then astronomers around the world turned to look.
shots: q: gamma ray burst flash animation

lines.say: In the glowing debris, their instruments found signs of heavy elements being made on the spot.
shots: line art: spectrum with lines highlighted

lines.say: Estimates suggested this one collision forged several Earth masses' worth of gold and platinum.
shots: line art: Earth icons stacked in gold

lines.say: Normal stars can't make much gold. It takes something this violent. Scientists still debate how much of the universe's gold comes from collisions like this, and how much from other explosions.
But some of the gold on your finger may have been made when two dead stars crashed, long before the Sun existed.

fact_note: GW170817, LIGO/Virgo, 17 Aug 2017 (KNOWN). ~130-140 Mly, NGC 4993 (KNOWN). GRB 1.7 s later, kilonova, r-process signatures (KNOWN). Gold yield estimates of several Earth masses (KNOWN as estimates, wide range). Share of r-process from mergers vs collapsars (DEBATED). Distinct from TTB's 'stardust/iron' reel: this is gold + neutron stars.
ig_caption: your wedding ring might literally be made of neutron star crash debris. we SAW one of these happen in 2017
tt_caption: where gold comes from: colliding neutron stars #space #astronomy

lines.say: In 1977, NASA launched two Voyager probes. Each carried a gold-plated record, meant for anyone who might find it.
shots: archive: Voyager Golden Record cover (NASA public domain)

lines.say: On it: greetings in fifty-five languages. Whales singing. Thunder. A heartbeat. A kiss.
Music from Bach to Chuck Berry. And the brainwaves of a woman named Ann Druyan, recorded while she thought about love.
It also carries a written message from the US president at the time, Jimmy Carter. Part of it says:
This is a present from a small, distant world, a token of our sounds, our science, our images, our music, our thoughts and our feelings.
shots: q: Earth from space slow rotation (NASA)

lines.say: We are attempting to survive our time so we may live into yours.
shots: q: city lights from orbit night (NASA)

lines.say: Voyager 1 left the solar system in 2012. The record should outlast every city on Earth.
shots: q: deep space starfield slow drift

fact_note: Voyager 1 & 2, 1977, Golden Record (KNOWN). 55 languages, whales, thunder, heartbeat, kiss, Bach, Chuck Berry, Ann Druyan EEG (KNOWN). Carter statement quoted verbatim (KNOWN). Voyager 1 heliopause crossing Aug 2012 (KNOWN). Durability claims (estimate). NASA images are public domain.
ig_caption: 'we are attempting to survive our time so we may live into yours'. a president wrote that to aliens in 1977 and it's still flying
tt_caption: what's on the Voyager Golden Record #voyager #space

lines.say: In 1950, at lunch in Los Alamos, the physicist Enrico Fermi was chatting with colleagues about flying saucers. Suddenly he asked: but where is everybody?
His point: our galaxy has hundreds of billions of stars, many older than the Sun. Even slow travelers could have spread across it by now.
shots: line art: dots spreading across galaxy

lines.say: So why don't we see anyone? Here are three of the most discussed answers.
One. Life is common, but intelligence is incredibly rare. We might be among the first.
Two. There's a great filter, some step almost no civilization survives. The scary question is whether it's behind us, or ahead.
shots: line art: funnel with few dots passing

lines.say: Three. They're out there, but too far apart in space or time. Two candles lit in a huge dark house, centuries apart.
shots: q: two candles in dark room far apart

lines.say: Nobody knows which one is true. But every answer says something huge about us.
shots: q: night sky observer silhouette telescope

fact_note: Fermi's 1950 Los Alamos lunch, 'Where is everybody?' (KNOWN, accounts by Teller, York, Konopinski). 100-400 billion stars (KNOWN range). Rare intelligence, Great Filter (Hanson 1996), spatial/temporal separation are hypotheses (SPECULATION).
ig_caption: the great filter one keeps me up at night. is it behind us or ahead of us
tt_caption: the Fermi paradox: where are all the aliens? #fermiparadox #aliens

lines.say: This is a computer printout from August 1977. Rows of numbers and letters from a radio telescope in Ohio called Big Ear.
shots: line art: redraw of printout columns

lines.say: A volunteer astronomer named Jerry Ehman was going through it days later. He saw six characters: 6EQUJ5. And he circled them in red pen, and wrote: Wow!
shots: q: red pen circling on paper

lines.say: Those characters meant a signal that rose and fell exactly like something from a fixed point in space passing through the telescope's view. Seventy-two seconds.
shots: line art: signal curve rising and falling

lines.say: It was close to the frequency of hydrogen, a frequency many scientists thought aliens might use to get noticed.
Astronomers pointed telescopes at that spot again and again for decades. It never came back.
In 2024, a team proposed a natural explanation: a cold hydrogen cloud suddenly brightened by a burst from a passing star.
shots: line art: cloud lit by flash

lines.say: It's the best explanation so far. It isn't proven. And the printout still says Wow.

fact_note: Wow! signal 15 Aug 1977, Big Ear (Ohio State), Jerry Ehman (KNOWN). 72 s transit, near 1420 MHz hydrogen line (KNOWN). Never repeated despite searches (KNOWN). Mendez et al. 2024 hydrogen-cloud maser-like brightening hypothesis (DEBATED). Printout image licence unclear: redraw.
ig_caption: a guy literally wrote 'Wow!' on the printout and nobody has topped that reaction in 49 years
tt_caption: the Wow! signal and the 2024 explanation #wowsignal #aliens

lines.say: Squeeze the whole history of the universe, thirteen point eight billion years, into one calendar year.
shots: q: Big Bang animation light burst

lines.say: January 1st, midnight: the Big Bang.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, forms in the spring. Our Sun and Earth don't show up until early September.
Life on Earth begins in late September. The dinosaurs arrive on Christmas Day and die out on December 30th.
Humans like us appear on December 31st, about eleven minutes before midnight.
All of written history, every empire, every war, every prophet, fits in the last eleven seconds.
Everything we argue about happened in eleven seconds, in a year that's mostly silence.

fact_note: Carl Sagan's Cosmic Calendar (1977) (KNOWN). Computed: 13.8 Gyr = 1 yr. Sun/Earth 4.6 Gyr -> ~Sep 1-2. Life ~3.8-4 Gyr -> late Sep. Dinosaurs 230-66 Myr -> Dec 25 / Dec 30. Humans 300k yr -> 11.4 min. Writing 5,000 yr -> 11.4 s. Milky Way formation 'spring' approx (thick disk/halo ages vary) (KNOWN approx).
ig_caption: if the universe was one year, all of recorded history is the last 11 seconds of New Year's Eve. kind of humbling
tt_caption: the history of the universe compressed into one year #space #cosmiccalendar

lines.say: Light is fast, but not instant. So everything you see, you see as it was, not as it is.
shots: q: light beam through dark room

lines.say: The person across the table: a few billionths of a second ago.
shots: q: coffee cup on table across

lines.say: The Moon: one and a third seconds ago.
The Sun: about eight minutes ago. If it vanished, you'd have eight more minutes of daylight before you knew.
The bright red star in Orion's shoulder, Betelgeuse: the light left it centuries ago, around the time of the Renaissance.
And on a dark night you can see a faint smudge in Andromeda. That light left two and a half million years ago, before our species existed.
When you look up at night, you're not looking out. You're looking back.
shots: q: Milky Way over mountains time-lapse

fact_note: Moon ~1.28 light-seconds, Sun ~8 min 20 s (KNOWN). Betelgeuse distance ~550-700 ly (DEBATED; 'centuries ago, around the Renaissance' fits 500-700 ly). Andromeda ~2.5 Mly, naked-eye visible in dark skies (KNOWN). Homo sapiens ~300k yr (KNOWN).
ig_caption: if the sun disappeared right now we'd have 8 more minutes of sunlight and no idea. thinking about this way too much
tt_caption: when you look at the stars you're looking into the past #space #light

lines.say: Everything you've ever seen: stars, planets, people, gas between galaxies. Add it all up, and it's about five percent of the universe.
The rest is stuff we've never directly detected.
About twenty-seven percent is dark matter. In the 1970s, Vera Rubin measured how fast stars orbit in galaxies. The outer ones move too fast. There isn't enough visible mass to hold them in.
shots: archive: Vera Rubin photo (public domain, verify)
line art: rotation curve flat vs expected

lines.say: Something invisible is adding gravity. We can see its effects, but not what it is.
shots: line art: invisible halo around galaxy

lines.say: And about sixty-eight percent is dark energy. In 1998, astronomers found the universe isn't just expanding, it's speeding up. Something is pushing it apart.
shots: line art: galaxies moving apart faster

lines.say: Dark matter and dark energy are names for what we don't understand. Ninety-five percent of reality is still a question mark.
shots: line art: big question mark over pie chart

fact_note: Planck 2018: ~5% ordinary matter, ~27% dark matter, ~68% dark energy (KNOWN). Rubin & Ford rotation curves 1970s (KNOWN; Zwicky 1933 earlier). Accelerating expansion 1998 (Riess, Perlmutter, Schmidt; Nobel 2011) (KNOWN). Nature of DM/DE unknown (KNOWN).
ig_caption: everything we've ever seen is 5% of the universe. the other 95% is basically 'we'll get back to you'
tt_caption: dark matter and dark energy explained simply #darkmatter #space

lines.say: In 1981, astronomers mapping galaxies toward the constellation Boötes found something unsettling. A hole.
shots: line art: galaxy map with empty circle

lines.say: A region of space roughly three hundred million light-years across, with almost nothing in it.
shots: q: empty dark space slow push
line art: scale bar 300 million ly

lines.say: To compare: our own galaxy is about a hundred thousand light-years wide. You could line up thousands of Milky Ways across it.
shots: line art: tiny galaxy icons in a row

lines.say: In a normal patch of space that size, you'd expect thousands of galaxies. In the Boötes Void, astronomers have found only around sixty.
shots: line art: sparse dots inside void

lines.say: It's called the Great Nothing. And it's not a mistake. The universe is built like foam: long threads of galaxies, and huge empty bubbles between them.
If we lived in the middle of it, the night sky would be nearly black, and we might not have known other galaxies existed for a very long time.

fact_note: Discovered by Kirshner, Oemler, Schechter, Shectman 1981 (KNOWN). Diameter ~250-330 Mly (KNOWN range; 'roughly 300'). ~60 galaxies found inside (KNOWN as reported). Cosmic web structure (KNOWN). Last line is a counterfactual (framed with 'might').
ig_caption: 300 million light years of almost nothing. imagine being born in the middle of that and looking up
tt_caption: the Bootes Void, the Great Nothing #space #universe

lines.say: In December 1995, astronomers did something that sounded like a waste of telescope time.
They pointed the Hubble Space Telescope at a tiny, empty-looking patch of sky in the Big Dipper. About the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length.
shots: line art: grain of sand at arm's length

lines.say: And they kept it there for ten days, collecting every bit of faint light.
This is what came back.
shots: archive: Hubble Deep Field (NASA public domain), full
archive: Hubble Deep Field slow push

lines.say: Almost every dot here is not a star. It's a galaxy. About three thousand of them, in that one speck of darkness.
shots: archive: Hubble Deep Field crop, galaxies

lines.say: Some of that light left its galaxy more than twelve billion years ago.
shots: archive: Hubble Ultra Deep Field crop (NASA)

lines.say: Point anywhere at the dark sky and look long enough, and it's full.
shots: archive: Hubble Deep Field pull back

fact_note: Hubble Deep Field, 18-28 Dec 1995, Ursa Major (KNOWN). Area ~1/24-millionth of sky (KNOWN; grain-of-sand analogy is NASA's). ~3,000 galaxies (KNOWN). Light >12 Gyr old in deep fields (KNOWN, Ultra Deep Field). NASA images public domain.
ig_caption: they aimed at the emptiest spot they could find and got 3,000 galaxies. every dot is a galaxy
tt_caption: the Hubble Deep Field, the most humbling photo ever taken #hubble #space

lines.say: Here's a question that bothered astronomers for centuries. Why is the night sky dark?
shots: q: dark night sky few stars
q: city at night looking up

lines.say: If the universe is endless and full of stars, then in every direction you look, your eye should eventually hit one. The whole sky should blaze like the Sun.
shots: line art: lines from eye hitting stars in every direction

lines.say: It's called Olbers' paradox, and for a long time nobody had a good answer.
Then, in 1848, a prose poem about the universe called Eureka came out. The author was Edgar Allan Poe.
shots: archive: Edgar Allan Poe daguerreotype (public domain)

lines.say: Poe suggested that the light from the most distant stars simply hasn't had time to reach us yet.
shots: line art: light still traveling toward Earth

lines.say: That's essentially part of the modern answer. The universe has an age, so we only see light that has had time to arrive, and expansion stretches the rest into darkness.
The man who wrote The Raven got a piece of cosmology right a century early.

fact_note: Olbers' paradox (1823; earlier Kepler, de Cheseaux) (KNOWN). Poe, 'Eureka: A Prose Poem', 1848, finite-light-travel explanation (KNOWN). Modern resolution: finite age + expansion/redshift (KNOWN). Poe's idea was speculative, not derived (note in copy tone).
ig_caption: the guy who wrote The Raven basically answered why the night sky is dark. in 1848. in a poem
tt_caption: Olbers' paradox and how Edgar Allan Poe guessed the answer #space #edgarallanpoe
